section_summaries.epidemiology: Chancroid was endemic in many developing countries, often introduced at seaports. By 2000, it largely disappeared from Eastern and Southern Africa and parts of Asia, where it once accounted for over 50% of genital ulcer disease. It flourished where men were uncircumcised and had unprotected sex with commercial sex workers. Its decline may be due to improved STI control during the HIV era and widespread quinolone use. Recently, H. ducreyi has been recognized in chronic cutaneous ulcers in children in South Sea Islands, Papua New Guinea, and Ghana, manifesting as painful ulcers that respond slowly to antimicrobials and accounting for 20-40% of "yawslike" leg ulcers. The reservoir is sexually active persons with genital ulcers, with a high attack rate (over 50% for men) after unprotected intercourse. H. ducreyi genital ulcers interact with HIV, increasing heterosexual transmission by recruiting and activating macrophages and T-helper lymphocytes, making individuals more susceptible to HIV infection, and increasing HIV excretion in genital discharge.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: As few as 30 H. ducreyi organisms can cause ulceration in human volunteers. Immunohistochemical analysis of ulcerating lesions shows a cell-mediated Th1 response primarily involving T lymphocytes and macrophages interstitially and perivascularly.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: After a 3-7 day incubation, an eroding genital ulcer develops. About 50% of chancroid ulcers are irregular, non-indurated, very painful lesions of variable depth with undermined edges and a yellow-gray purulent, readily bleeding exudative base; surrounding skin is usually not inflamed. Other presentations include giant ulcers from merging smaller ones, tiny dwarf ulcers mimicking genital herpes, transient superficial ulcers resembling lymphogranuloma venereum, a single painless ulcer confused with syphilis, and beefy, raised, indurated lesions appearing like granuloma inguinale. The site varies, with half on the prepuce in uncircumcised men and common kissing lesions. In women, most lesions are on the fourchette, labia, and perineal area. About 30% of patients develop painful inguinal adenitis which can progress to bubo formation with erythema, potentially rupturing into an abscess. "Yawslike" cutaneous ulcers in multiple South Sea Islands, Papua New Guinea, and Ghana represent a new presentation requiring further description.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Specimens for culture should be plated directly or transported at 4°C and plated within 24 hours on gonococcal agar with vancomycin (3 mg/L), 2% hemoglobin, 1% vitamin enrichment, and 0.25% charcoal. Incubation is at 32°C in 100% humidity and a CO2-enriched environment (e.g., candle extinction jar with a moist paper towel). Small, yellow-gray colonies appear after 2-5 days. Nucleic acid technologies are sensitive and specific for diagnosis.
section_summaries.treatment: H. ducreyi readily acquires plasmids, leading to rapid development and spread of antimicrobial resistance to drugs like tetracycline, ampicillin, sulfonamides, trimethoprim, kanamycin, streptomycin, and chloramphenicol. Effective regimens include Erythromycin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days, or a single 1-g dose of azithromycin, or a single 250-mg intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone (though failures occur in HIV co-infected patients). Ciprofloxacin and other fluoroquinolones are effective, with 95% cure rates after a 3-day regimen. Fluctuant buboes should be incised or aspirated.
section_summaries.prevention: Due to the link between chancroid and explosive heterosexual HIV transmission, its control and elimination are priorities. Enhanced STI control strategies should include effective syndromic treatment at first contact, increased condom use (especially by sex workers), programs for prostitute care/treatment, and partner referral. Rapid response to outbreaks is vital in national STI control programs to prevent re-introduction and re-endemification. Continued efforts are needed to control chancroid's role in facilitating HIV transmission. Strategies for chronic leg ulcers due to H. ducreyi also need to be developed, requiring better understanding of their epidemiology.
